correctness.rationale: Verified the Cayley deletion bijection for each named cherry, the uniform reduced-tree law, the resulting conditional Wiener expectation, exact path-count and tail identities for the mean Wiener index, and the exact covariance by indicator linearity. The sign proof partitions the integers exhaustively: full exact-rational checks \(4\le n\le626\); analytic product-telescope bound for \(n\ge627\). Boundary \(n=2,3\) and a total of 18,247 Prüfer-tree enumerations \(3\le n\le7\) agree. A dominated Gaussian Riemann-sum argument yields the stated asymptotic. Finite checks are not taken as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The full-text comparison finds the distinguished-cherry marginal in Erdős–Rényi and Wiener/mixed path-length results in Janson, but no theorem yielding the exact all-size cherry–Wiener covariance, universal sign, and scale. Separate-result implications, probabilistic models, and center-degree conventions were explicitly differentiated. Targeted semantic and exact-phrase literature searches produced no same-object equivalent or dominating formula; historical joint-index coverage remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: An older joint enumerator of tree distance profiles and motif counts might imply this result after differentiation, even if the exact pair is not named.
The 1994 Entringer–Meir–Moon–Székely Wiener-index paper was confirmed bibliographically but its complete text was not materially inspected; its stated focus is mean Wiener indices.
The originality conclusion concerns the inspected literature and searchable records, not unpublished results.

value.rationale: A cherry is the elementary symmetry-inducing leaf motif of a Cayley tree, whereas the Wiener index quantifies global pairwise distances. The exact sign for every nontrivial size and the \(n^{5/2}\) covariance scale quantify how local symmetry-bearing structure globally changes distances. The conditioning identity exposes the mechanism and is not determined by the two well-studied marginal expectations; this is a natural dependence question, not an arbitrary parameter slice.
